description: We're Electrical Engineering and Physics students, combining strong technical skills, a solid understanding of physics, and, of course, the power of friendship!
summary: SPHEREx Sky Flip-book is a web tool that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change. A user picks any patch of sky, and the tool fetches NASA’s real SPHEREx photos of it, lines them up, and combines the hundred or so photos from each six-month sky pass into one clean frame, always using the same mix of infrared colours so that a difference between frames means the sky changed and not the camera. The frames play as a short flip-book in which moving and varying objects stand out: fast nearby stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids and comets. Clicking any object shows its spectrum for each pass, a plain-language label of what it probably is, and automatic checks against known catalogues (Gaia, CatWISE, 2MASS, Pan-STARRS, SIMBAD) and against NASA’s asteroid data, so the user can tell a known object from an unexplained one worth reporting. Chemistry filters highlight molecules such as methane and water ice, and older photos from NASA’s WISE (2010) and the Canadian Space Agency’s NEOSSat stretch the timeline to 16 years. A “Spot the mover” game trains new volunteers on known examples, and every view can be shared as a link. The tool was verified on Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis, and it follows the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS in both SPHEREx and NEOSSat data.
details:
SPHEREx Sky Flip-book lets anyone pick a patch of sky on a 3D globe and watch NASA’s SPHEREx photos of it as a flip-book across the telescope’s six-month passes.

How it works: the tool fetches every SPHEREx photo of the chosen spot from NASA’s IRSA archive, lines them up, and builds each frame from the same mix of infrared colours, so a steady star stays steady and only real changes stand out.

What you can do: play or step through the frames, subtract passes to see only what changed, click any object for its spectrum in each pass, switch on chemistry filters (methane, water ice, CO2), let the computer search for moving objects, check finds against known catalogues (Gaia, CatWISE and others), and export pictures and data.

Results: it measured Barnard’s Star moving 10.2 arcseconds per year (true value 10.4), found the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855 with no hint where to look, and detected the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS in both SPHEREx and Canada’s NEOSSat telescope (CSA data from the CADC archive).

Impact: the public, classrooms and researchers can spot moving and changing objects that are too many for professionals to inspect by eye. Known asteroids are shown with NASA’s published risk data.

Tools: Python (Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI) and a browser front end (three.js, Plotly.js).

Use of AI: the code was written with Anthropic’s Claude, an AI assistant, under our direction. We chose the approach and checked the results against known values. No AI runs inside the tool, and no images are AI-generated.

Limits: finds are candidates, not confirmed discoveries. The tool currently runs on a local computer.
dataRefs: WISE and CatWISE at NASA IRSA
